items.title: Heat, lost income, and violence: How Chennai women are bearing the cost of a hotter city
items.summary: The kathrikka (brinjal) curry was bubbling in a large aluminium pot, sending up the smell of fried onions and spices into the narrow lane outside Kalaivani’s one-room home. She chopped another handful of onions, stirred the curry, and checked the flame, moving between the chores without pausing. Around her, dirty water trickled through the lane. A few metres away, tiny, dark rooms that stored animal hides filled the air with a heavy stench. Further ahead stood a large cattle shed, where women worked on the hides left behind after slaughter. This is Puliyanthope in North Chennai, where generations of families, many of them Dalit and Muslim, live alongside slaughterhouses, tanneries, and the waste that comes with them. But for Kalaivani, the hardest part of living here is not the filth or the stench. It is the heat. “In summer, it is not possible to go to work or sit at home. It is boiling hot inside my house. At night, I am not able to sleep properly. I wake up multiple times and pour water all over my body,” she said. By morning, she is exhausted. “The next day, I don’t even feel like getting up.
